label: Mean, Median, Mode & Range
overview: Measures of center (mean, median, mode) and spread (range) summarize a data set with a single number. SAT questions ask you to compute these values, compare them, or determine how adding/removing a value changes them. Understanding what each measure represents — and how outliers affect it — is just as important as knowing the formulas.

keyFormulas.name: Median
keyFormulas.latex: \text{Middle value when data is sorted; average of two middle values if even count}

workedExamples.problem: A student's test scores are 72, 85, 90, 68, and 95. What is the mean score? What is the median?

steps.title: Compute the mean
steps.content: Add all scores, then divide by the count (5).

steps.title: Find the median
steps.content: Sort the scores: 68, 72, 85, 90, 95. The middle value (3rd of 5) is 85.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to sort the data before finding the median
commonMistakes.fix: Always sort first. Finding the 'middle' of unsorted data gives the wrong answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using the count of the whole group when only a subset is summed
commonMistakes.fix: Check what the denominator should be — it is the count of the values you are averaging, not any other group size.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing mean and median when an outlier is present
commonMistakes.fix: An extreme value pulls the mean toward it but barely moves the median. If one very large (or small) value exists, the median is more representative.

quickTip: Use the 'balance point' idea: mean is where the data balances; median is the physical middle. An outlier tilts the balance but not the middle.
